description: Keynotes, mitigation bypasses, and research disclosures from the inaugural DEF CON China Beta in Beijing.

talks.title: Bugs Aren't Random: Unifying Building & Breaking in the Modern Age
talks.teaser: Dan Kaminsky examines why software engineering fails to deliver the predictability of physical engineering disciplines and proposes unifying builders and breakers.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Software engineering consistently fails to achieve the structural predictability and mechanical resilience found in traditional engineering disciplines. Decades of vulnerability research demonstrate that developers and attackers repeatedly discover and exploit identical flaw classes. This recurring dynamic suggests that bugs are not anomalous or random events, but rather the predictable output of tools and engineering abstractions that isolate creators from runtime consequences.

Vulnerability Analysis

The fundamental boundary separating developers from testers, forward engineers from reverse engineers, and humans from automated tooling fosters systematic weaknesses. Current systems reward rapid feature delivery while obscuring failure domains, allowing subtle state inconsistencies and memory bugs to survive undetected until adversaries probe them.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Kaminsky analyzes how traditional fuzzing and testing paradigms uncover vulnerabilities without solving the structural patterns enabling them. Drawing upon real-world case studies and operational proof-of-concept implementations, the presentation challenges conventional assumptions regarding the separation of construction and exploitation.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Defenders and architects must adopt architectures where building and breaking are unified continuously. By integrating automated vulnerability discovery into development workflows and rethinking hardware and software contracts, engineering organizations can eliminate entire vulnerability classes at root.

talks.title: Evolution of the Hacker Community in Asia
talks.teaser: Jayson E. Street chronicles the history, ethos, and shared identity uniting the hacker community across Asia and the global cybersecurity ecosystem.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

The global hacker community thrives on curiosity, continuous learning, and collaborative problem-solving across geographical and linguistic borders. As information security expanded across Asia, local communities established distinct traditions while maintaining deep philosophical ties with the broader international movement.

Vulnerability Analysis

Misunderstandings regarding the term "hacker" often create friction between technical practitioners, corporations, and the public. Stereotypes obscure the ethical foundations and defensive contributions of security researchers, emphasizing isolated criminal activity rather than systemic resilience and community education.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Street explores the historical milestones of pioneering Chinese and Asian hackers through field experiences, anecdotes, and cultural analysis. He highlights how grassroots meetups, DEF CON Groups, and regional capture-the-flag competitions fostered technical excellence and cross-border partnerships.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Strengthening cybersecurity requires nurturing inclusive, community-driven spaces where researchers can share disclosures safely. By embracing the ethical hacker ethos and mentoring emerging talent, global infosec collectives can collectively defend critical digital infrastructure.

talks.title: Spreading Malware with Google: Nice Quilombo
talks.teaser: Fabian Cuchietti and Gonzalo Sanchez demonstrate how Google Earth can be abused for in-memory malware injection, sandbox evasion, and cryptomining.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Trusted desktop applications from reputable vendors often receive broad permissions and minimal scrutiny from endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents. Google Earth features advanced rendering engines, scripting capabilities, and embedded web components designed to deliver dynamic geographic visualizations.

Vulnerability Analysis

The researchers uncover an attack chain within Google Earth that allows adversaries to bypass client-side security sandboxes. By manipulating document handlers and memory management routines, an attacker can load arbitrary payloads directly into the execution context of trusted Google processes.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Cuchietti and Sanchez demonstrate three specific exploitation scenarios: hijacking authenticated Google sessions, gaining remote code execution via interactive shells, and executing stealthy in-memory JavaScript malware configured for unauthorized Monero cryptocurrency mining without triggering disk-based heuristics.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Mitigating trusted-application abuse requires strict memory integrity controls, behavioral monitoring of child process spawning, and hardening sandbox boundaries for embedded WebViews. Security teams should enforce application whitelisting and monitor suspicious parent-child process relationships across productivity tools.

talks.title: You Logged into My Account
talks.teaser: Daizibukaikou details login cross-site request forgery and account-takeover vectors where attackers induce victims to authenticate into malicious sessions.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Modern web platforms rely on federated identity standards such as OAuth and Single Sign-On (SSO) alongside cookie-based session management to streamline user authentication. While traditional attacks focus on stealing user credentials, forcing a victim to authenticate into an attacker-controlled account represents a dangerous but frequently overlooked vector.

Vulnerability Analysis

Login CSRF and unvalidated OAuth state parameters enable adversaries to pre-authenticate a victim's browser into the attacker's profile. Once logged in, any private information, financial transactions, or third-party accounts linked by the victim become permanently accessible to the attacker.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Daizibukaikou demonstrates practical attack workflows chaining login CSRF, self-XSS, and flawed OAuth redirect flows across major internet platforms. The attacker induces the victim into linking personal services, stealing session tokens, exposing privacy data, and executing fraudulent identity binding.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Developers must implement strict CSRF tokens on login and logout endpoints, enforce state verification during OAuth handshakes, and explicitly prompt users when linking secondary accounts. Session regeneration on privilege changes and robust cross-origin isolation mitigate forced authentication vulnerabilities.

talks.title: Androsia: Securing Data in Process for Your Android Apps
talks.teaser: Samit Anwer presents Androsia, an automated tool utilizing interprocedural data flow analysis and bytecode rewriting to eliminate secrets lingering in Android memory.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Each Android application executes in an isolated runtime environment with finite heap memory managed by a garbage collector. The Android runtime does not distinguish between ordinary objects and security-sensitive constructs such as cryptographic keys, session tokens, or personal identifiers.

Vulnerability Analysis

Java does not provide deterministic object destruction APIs, causing security-critical data to linger in process memory indefinitely until system memory pressure triggers garbage collection. During this retention window, runtime memory dumps, side-channel attacks, or local process compromises can extract unencrypted secrets.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Anwer highlights the inadequacy of standard java.security APIs for zeroing memory and demonstrates how secrets persist across heap allocations. He introduces Androsia, an open-source static analysis and bytecode transformation framework that performs interprocedural data flow analysis to pinpoint where sensitive objects are last referenced, automatically injecting bytecode that wipes secret values.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Mobile developers should adopt automated bytecode instrumentation during build pipelines to overwrite sensitive memory structures immediately following usage. Combining deterministic zeroization with secure hardware-backed keystores minimizes the attack window for in-memory credential harvesting.

talks.title: Lessons Learned from Five Years of DEF CON CTF
talks.teaser: Vito Genovese shares architectural, engineering, and organizational lessons from five years designing and executing DEF CON CTF with Legitimate Business Syndicate.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

DEF CON Capture the Flag (CTF) represents the pinnacle of competitive hacking, pitting world-class teams against complex attack-and-defense services. Operating a reliable, tamper-resistant competition platform under relentless adversary assault requires robust distributed infrastructure and disciplined operational planning.

Vulnerability Analysis

Organizing high-stakes CTF competitions introduces unique failure modes: scoring system manipulation, routing and network saturation attacks, unexpected zero-days in challenge architectures, and team coordination breakdowns under extreme multi-day stress.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Genovese details the five-year operational history of Legitimate Business Syndicate (LegitBS), breaking down iconic challenge architectures, scoring algorithm evolutions, and the high-availability infrastructure required to sustain intense player traffic. He shares real-world postmortems of unintended challenge solves and emergency live patches.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

CTF organizers should implement containerized challenge isolation, comprehensive telemetry pipelines, redundant scoring backends, and decoupled game states. Maintaining healthy team dynamics and post-competition retrospectives ensures sustainable community-led event operations.

talks.title: Blasted Bits
talks.teaser: Zoz tests forensic-resistant rapid physical destruction of magnetic and flash media using thermal, kinetic, high-voltage, and explosive methods.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Retiring sensitive digital storage media safely is critical for enterprises, governments, and individuals facing sophisticated physical threats. Standard degaussing or cryptographic wiping methods often require extensive time and controlled facility environments, leaving media vulnerable to seizure or trash harvesting.

Vulnerability Analysis

Residual magnetic flux and semiconductor charge states can often be recovered using specialized laboratory equipment and electron microscopy unless media is completely destroyed at a molecular or crystal-lattice level. In emergency scenarios, defenders require instantaneous, fail-safe elimination of storage units.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Zoz explores rapid, forensic-resistant media elimination mechanisms capable of neutralizing magnetic platters and solid-state flash memory in under 60 seconds. Through rigorous experimental testing, he evaluates thermal reactions, kinetic impacts, high-voltage discharges, and custom 3D-printed explosive encapsulation systems.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Organizations handling high-consequence data should establish multilayered media sanitation protocols that combine full-disk cryptographic erasure with certified mechanical pulverization or thermal destruction systems. Emergency zeroization devices must be engineered with robust failsafes to prevent accidental deployment.

talks.title: I Am Groot: Examining the Guardians of Windows 10 Security
talks.teaser: Chuanda Ding dissects the internal architecture of Windows 10 security mitigations and explains how advanced exploit techniques bypass Defender protections.
talks.summary:
Architecture and Background

Following successive Pwn2Own competitions, Microsoft systematically fortified Windows 10 and Microsoft Edge by integrating layered exploit mitigations throughout the kernel and user-mode execution subsystems. These protections, frequently branded under the Windows Defender Guard suite, aim to disrupt common exploit primitives.

Vulnerability Analysis

Exploitation defenses including Control Flow Guard (CFG), Arbitrary Code Guard (ACG), and Code Integrity Guard (CIG) introduce architectural barriers against memory corruption, return-oriented programming (ROP), and unapproved dynamic executable memory allocation. Understanding the boundary limitations of these guards is essential for both defense and offensive research.

Exploitation and Demonstrations

Ding delivers an insider technical breakdown of Windows 10 mitigation internals based on real-world exploit development and Pwn2Own competitive findings. He demonstrates how sophisticated attackers bypass security controls through data-only attacks, indirect call manipulation, and sandbox escape chains.

Remediation and Defensive Strategies

Enterprise defenders should enforce hardware-enforced stack protection, enable Virtualization-based Security (VBS), and configure Windows Defender Exploit Guard policies across all critical endpoints. Continuously validating mitigations against emerging evasion techniques ensures comprehensive platform defense.
